'''Sarah Davis Baker''' is a video essayist whose YouTube channel publishes, in her own description, "slightly haunted essays about the internet, memory, and the things people leave behind." The channel began in late 2021 — her earliest uploads were about cats — and grew into one of the quieter, more atmospheric corners of the video-essay world, with some work appearing early or exclusively on Nebula. She is included in [[Media and Personalities]] as a '''YouTuber entry''': a look at what she actually makes and why people watch, rather than an ideological audit.

== What she makes ==

Her essays sit at the seam of philosophy, internet culture, and a gentle strain of horror — less "explainer," more mood. Recurring themes run through the catalog: '''decay and what outlasts us''' (the internet as a place of abandoned pages and left-behind selves), '''isolation and enclosure''', '''the uncanny''', and the strangeness of being perceived. The tone is essayistic and unhurried; the "haunted" in her own tagline is the right word for it.

== Notable videos and series ==

A representative run of her work shows the range and the throughlines:

* ''The Horror of Impossible Architecture'' — spaces that cannot exist, and why they unsettle us.
* ''The Haunted Universe'' — cosmic-scale dread in the essay form.
* ''Bunkers, Vaults & Biospheres'' — enclosure, survival, and the human urge to seal ourselves in.
* ''The Robot Body'' and ''The Uncanny Horror of AI Hallucinations'' — the machine, the almost-human, and what goes wrong at the edges of the uncanny valley.
* ''The Persistence of Decay'' — things rotting, fading, and refusing to fully disappear.
* ''Why Being Seen Feels Like Hell: Sartre, Shame, and No Exit'' — philosophy brought down to the lived feeling of being watched.

== Why she fits the Library ==

Her preoccupations — memory, the uncanny, the robot body, AI's hallucinations, what persists after a thing is gone — rhyme with threads the rest of this Library takes seriously: machine consciousness ([[The Decades Brain]], [[Hathor]]), the uncanny and the sacred, and the question of what a self is when it is distributed or left behind ([[Egregore]]). We point to her as a well-made example of the essay form working that seam, not as a source of doctrine.
